questions.q: Put these steps in the order the priority ladder suggests, first to last.
items: Join the workplace pension, at least up to the employer match
Clear credit card and overdraft debt
Build three to six months of essential costs
Invest for the long term in a Stocks and Shares ISA
questions.why: Protect yourself, take free money, stop expensive debt, finish the safety net, then invest money you won't need for years.

questions.q: Sam, 23, has £300 in the bank, £1,200 on a card at 29% APR, and wants to start investing £100 a month. What's the best next step?
options: Build a small emergency buffer and put the £100 towards the card until it's cleared
Start investing straight away; markets beat 29% over time
Pay only the card minimum and invest the rest
Stop paying the card to save faster
questions.why: Clearing 29% debt is a guaranteed 29% return; investing can't promise that. Never miss minimum payments.

questions.q: You want {g} for a car in {m} months. Ignoring interest, how much must you save each month? (To the nearest pound.)
questions.why: {g} ÷ {m} = {answer} a month. Put it on a standing order for payday.

questions.topic: the right home for each goal
questions.q: Match each goal to where the money would usually sit.
questions.why: Short timeframes need cash that can't fall in value; long timeframes can ride out ups and downs for higher expected growth.

questions.q: Someone in England earns {s} a year with no pension or loan. What's their yearly take-home pay after income tax (20%) and NI (8%) on pay above £12,570?
Someone with a small credit card balance should still usually stay in their workplace pension at the minimum.
questions.why: The employer contribution and tax relief roughly double their money immediately, which beats card interest. They just shouldn't pay extra into the pension until the card is cleared.

questions.topic: ISAs and the Personal Savings Allowance
questions.q: A basic-rate taxpayer with £2,000 in savings is choosing between a Cash ISA paying 3.8% and a normal saver paying 4.5%. Which usually wins?
options: The 4.5% saver: £90 of interest is under the £1,000 Personal Savings Allowance anyway
The Cash ISA, because ISAs always win
The Cash ISA, because normal savings are taxed at 20%
Neither: keep it in a current account
questions.why: Interest under the Personal Savings Allowance is already tax-free, so the higher rate wins.

questions.q: A graduate on Plan 5 earns {s}. What's their monthly student loan repayment?
questions.why: 9% of pay above £25,000, divided by 12: {answer} a month.

questions.q: When is a good regular time to review a financial plan, and why?
options: Each April, when the new tax year brings new allowances and rates
Never: a good plan doesn't need changing
questions.why: Tax figures, ISA allowances and pension thresholds change from 6 April, and a yearly review keeps goals current.

questions.q: Explain why the priority ladder puts long-term investing after an emergency fund and clearing expensive debt.

ideas.label: Investments can fall, so money you might need soon shouldn't be invested; an emergency fund stops you selling at a bad time or borrowing
Expensive debt costs more than investments are likely to earn

questions.model: Investments can fall in value, so money you might need soon shouldn't be in them: without an emergency fund you might have to sell at a bad time or borrow. And expensive debt at around 30% costs far more than investments are likely to earn, so clearing it first is a guaranteed better return.
questions.why: Investing works best on money you won't need for years, with no expensive debt dragging against it.

tests.answer: Investments can go down so you need an emergency fund first, and card debt costs more than investing would earn.
Because you need to be older to invest.

questions.q: Explain why writing rules in advance (for pay rises, windfalls, card use) helps a plan work.

ideas.label: The decision is already made, so you don't rely on willpower or mood in the moment
It stops spending rising to match extra money (lifestyle creep)

questions.model: If the rule is set in advance, the decision is already made, so you don't have to rely on willpower when you're tempted. It stops spending quietly rising to swallow every pay rise or windfall.
questions.why: Decide once, calmly, instead of every time under temptation.

tests.answer: The decision is made in advance so you don't rely on willpower, and it stops lifestyle creep when you get a pay rise.
So you don't just spend extra money.
